Anthony Aguilar, retired Army lieutenant colonel, says the rehearsal is over:

Why haul that much firepower halfway around the world if nobody plans to use it?

SAILORS FIRST SUNDAY: Sailor Of The Week ⚓

Congratulations to HM2 Brandon W. Williams, a Colorado native who serves as the SAR Medical Technician Standardization Leading Petty Officer (LPO) with Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron Two-Five (HSC-25) in Agana, Guam!

As medical department LPO, he led five HMs and advised one Senior Medical Officer in FDNF command medical readiness, pre/post deployment medical requirements, and medical training for 435 sailors from HSC-25, AIMD, ASD, AIMD Bahrain, VUP-19, and ERCS Naval Hospital Guam. 

His leadership resulted in treating 560 patients, inoculating 125 service members from Influenza, Japanese Encephalitis and Hepatitis, 18 flight physicals, 109 post-deployment health assessments and 53 pre-deployment health screenings, contributing to 92% squadron medical readiness, as well as the deployment of Detachment 3 and Detachment 6 in support of ESB-6/ LHA-7.

As a Search and Rescue Medical Technician, Williams responded directly to two Medevacs, including one stroke patient that required urgent intervention to prevent neurological deterioration and one renal failure patient that required higher-level care, impacting two souls saved. cvn-71.t: ⚓️‼️ The US Navy Cannot Sustain A Significant Naval Presence in the Arabian Sea Many observers are worked up today about the old news that CSG-9 (USS Theodore…
cvn-71.tx:
⚓️‼️ The US Navy Cannot Sustain A Significant Naval Presence in the Arabian Sea

Many observers are worked up today about the old news that CSG-9 (USS Theodore Roosevelt CVN-71) is headed to the Arabian Sea.

What most people are failing to understand is that the US Navy simply does not have the capability to sustain even a 2-carrier fleet in the Arabian Sea, let alone a 3-carrier fleet including 2 amphibious ready groups, 2 cruisers, and 10 destroyers.

As best I can ascertain, the US warship count in the region (counting the not-yet-arrived CSG-9) would be:

3 aircraft carriers: ~15,000 mouths
2 amphibious ready groups: ~8000 
2 cruisers: ~700
10 destroyers: ~3250

That makes a total of ~27,000 mouths that need to be fed 3x/day.

The closest bases are thousands of miles away.

The recent disastrous extended deployments of the USS Gerald R. Ford and the USS Abraham Lincoln underscore what happens on these big ships after extended deployments. Things go to hell in a handbasket, and sailors start jumping off the decks to escape the madness.

I consider it not only unlikely, but very likely physically impossible for the US to sustain 3 carrier strike groups for more than just a few weeks near Iran — not now, nor at any time in the foreseeable future.

Could they briefly station a 3-carrier fleet in the region with the intent to launch a week or two of attacks against Iranian targets? Sure. It could be done for a short period of time.

But if they attempt to do this, I predict we will finally see the Iranians make a determined effort to strike US warships, and they will succeed. The US Navy will be exposed as a 20th century relic incapable of fighting a 21st century war.

cvn-71.t: A multibillion-rupee F-35C fighter jet attempted to land on the USS Theodore Roosevelt but failed to catch an arresting cable, forcing the pilot to take off ag…
cvn-71.tx:
A multibillion-rupee F-35C fighter jet attempted to land on the USS Theodore Roosevelt but failed to catch an arresting cable, forcing the pilot to take off again. The footage reportedly shows an F/A-18F Super Hornet landing successfully before the F-35C’s unsuccessful attempt.

Aircraft carriers use arresting cables stretched across the flight deck. A fighter jet’s tailhook must catch one of these cables to bring the aircraft to a stop within the short landing area. If the hook misses every cable, the pilot must immediately power up and climb away.

This is known as a “bolter.” It is a recognised part of carrier aviation, not necessarily a sign of aircraft malfunction. With a short deck, tight timing and little room for error, carrier landings remain among the most demanding operations in military aviation.

The ships are expected to arrive by the end of November, adding about 10,000 sailors and Marines to the region. Fox News reports about 6,000 are in the carrier strike group and about 4,200 in the MEU and Makin Island group.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt would be the third aircraft carrier in the Middle East, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. The USS Makin Island would be the second amphibious assault ship with an embarked MEU in the region, alongside USS Boxer and the 11th MEU.

lhd-4.t: If you want to understand what it means to be an American citizen, look at what happened in the Indian Ocean on Easter Sunday, April 12, 2009. One merchant cap…
lhd-4.tx:
If you want to understand what it means to be an American citizen, look at what happened in the Indian Ocean on Easter Sunday, April 12, 2009.

One merchant captain from Vermont named Richard Phillips was being held hostage inside a covered orange lifeboat by Somali pirates armed with AK-47s.

He was not a general. He was not a politician. He was one cargo ship captain who had offered himself as a hostage to save his crew.

To bring that one man home, the United States sent the guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, the frigate USS Halyburton, the amphibious assault ship USS Boxer, and a team of U.S. Navy SEALs who parachuted straight into the black ocean at night.

For four days, the lifeboat pitched violently in rough seas twenty-five yards behind the destroyer.

Then at dusk on Sunday, a pirate pressed the barrel of his AK-47 directly against Captain Phillips' back and prepared to kill him.

On the fantail of the USS Bainbridge, three Navy SEAL snipers lay braced in the dark. The destroyer was rolling in one direction. The tiny lifeboat was pitching in another. If even one sniper missed by half an inch, or fired a tenth of a second late, the hostage would die.

Through night-vision scopes, all three snipers waited for the exact millisecond when three targets appeared in the tiny windows at once.

One word came over the headset.

Three rifles fired as a single sound.

All three kidnappers dropped instantly. Captain Phillips walked onto the deck of the USS Bainbridge without a scratch.

Do not touch a citizen of a country that will drop Navy SEALs from the sky at midnight for one man.

The aircraft carrier group is due to arrive in the Middle East by the end of November.
New US naval deployments to the Middle East could expand President Donald Trump's military options as his administration weighs additional strikes on Iran.
The Pentagon is sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit to the Middle East, two US officials confirmed on Tuesday.
The USS Makin Island amphibious ready group also departed San Diego, carrying the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit.
Currently, two other US aircraft carriers are deployed in the region, namely the USS George H. W. Bush, which arrived in April, and the USS George Washington, which arrived in August to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln.
In addition, the USS Boxer amphibious ready group is deployed in the Arabian Sea, carrying the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit, alongside the USS Portland and USS Comstock.
Meanwhile, the US military has been conducting routine troop rotations in recent weeks, and additional troops and aircraft are expected to arrive in the coming weeks as part of preparations for an escalation in the Middle East, security sources told Walla on October 4.
Some 3,000 US troops are currently stationed across Israel. Their duties include operating air defense systems, serving as pilots and support crews, and handling logistics and headquarters operations.

qt.t:
🇺🇸 U.S. Navy has doubled its fleet capacity to operate the MQ-25A Stingray unmanned aircraft system (UAS) over a five-month period, standing up a second operational MD-5C Ground Control Station (GCS). @USNavy 

MD-5C, powered by Lockheed Martin Skunk Works MDCX autonomy platform, is installed in the Unmanned Air Warfare Center (UAWC), the dedicated shipboard command center for unmanned carrier aviation. The Navy's Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) received the first operational MD-5C in March 2026, followed by her sister ship USS Ronald Reagan (CVN 76) in August 2026. @LockheedMartin 

The MD-5C is a highly complex system-of-systems, which includes the government Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence (C4I) network, MDCX software and hardware, and additional government-produced ancillary equipment. Within the GCS, MDCX is the mission planning and execution software that enables Navy operators to command and control the MQ-25A Stingray, extending carrier air wing reach and freeing manned aircraft for higher-priority missions.

#USNavy #MQ25A #MD5C #MDCX #LockheedMartin #SkunkWorks

cvn-76.tx:
🇺🇸 Boeing, U.S. Navy and Lockheed Martin MQ-25 Integrated Test Team (ITT) established a beyond-line-of-sight (BLOS) satellite command-and-control (C2) link between the MQ-25A Stingray uncrewed aerial fefueler and a production MD-5C control station aboard aircraft carrier USS Ronald Reagan while the ship operated at port and at sea. @BoeingDefense @USNavy @LockheedMartin 

This marked the first time the aircraft was controlled from a carrier using the ground control station and Navy communications network used in operational missions.

The test validated an end-to-end BLOS C2 capability over the Navy’s operational command, control, communications, computers, and intelligence (C4I) network enabling shipboard teams can reliably monitor and command the MQ-25A from an aircraft carrier.

This demonstration is one in a series of buildup exercises designed to validate procedures, networks and interfaces ahead of a risk reduction flight-test program that will include carrier at-sea operations.

#USNavy #Boeing #MQ25A #MD5C

🇮🇷| The Day the Aircraft Carrier Retreated: How Iran Rewrote the Rules of Naval Warfare

On February 28, 2026, war broke out. The U.S. Navy deployed carrier strike groups to the Arabian Sea and the Red Sea. This was a pattern Washington had relied upon repeatedly over the past three decades: an aircraft carrier appears, the adversary backs down, a diplomatic solution is reached, and the carrier returns home.

This time, the carrier retreated.

💥 The Withdrawal of the USS Dwight D. Eisenhower

The carrier strike group centered on the USS *Dwight D. Eisenhower* was deployed to the Red Sea in the early stages of the conflict. Its mission: to protect Israel from Iranian missile strikes, ensure the safety of shipping in the Red Sea, and exert military pressure on Iran.

It failed to accomplish its mission. It retreated.

Iran’s arsenal, a combination of anti-ship ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, drones, swarms of fast attack craft, and naval mines was not designed to "sink an aircraft carrier." Rather, it was intended to render the carrier incapable of operating safely within the combat zone. If an aircraft carrier’s escort vessels must constantly intercept incoming missiles; if its carrier-based aircraft are forced to prioritize air defense over offensive strike missions; and if the carrier itself must repeatedly pull back to stay out of missile range then it has lost its core function: the projection of power.

The retreat of the *Eisenhower* was not a "tactical adjustment." It was a "failure of power projection."

🎯 East of Djibouti: A New Geographic Boundary

For the past two decades, Iranian military planners have grappled with a single question: How can the U.S. Navy be denied access to the Strait of Hormuz?

The answer is not simply "laying mines in the Strait." The answer lies in pushing the defensive line well to the east of the Strait. Iran’s anti-ship missiles cover the northern Arabian Sea, while its drones patrol even further afield. From bases along the coast of the Gulf of Oman, Iranian fast-attack craft guided by satellite and radar data can launch saturation attacks against any vessel that enters their range.

The U.S. Navy’s carrier strike groups have been forced to operate east of Djibouti. This is not a "strategic choice." This is "denial."

📜 "The Arabian Sea Will Be Cleared of Enemies"

On September 28, 2026, the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, stated: "The Arabian Sea, too, will soon be cleared of enemies."

This statement is not a prophecy; it is an acknowledgment of facts that have already come to pass.

The U.S. Navy’s deployment in the Arabian Sea has regressed from "forward presence" to "long-range deterrence." Its vessels no longer approach the Strait of Hormuz. Its aircraft carriers no longer enter the Red Sea. Fifty-four of its MQ-9 drones have been shot down. Its efforts to escort oil tankers have failed to prevent ships which have switched off their tracking transponders from striking naval mines and exploding.

"Cleared" does not mean "sunk." It means "rendered incapable of operating safely in this region."

⚔️ Rewriting the Rules of Naval Warfare

For the past seventy years, U.S. Naval doctrine has been built upon the assumption that carrier strike groups can operate freely in any maritime theater across the globe. This assumption relies on the premises that adversaries lack the capability to detect, track, and strike aircraft carriers; that they cannot launch saturation attacks from outside the carriers' defensive perimeters; and that they cannot withstand the retaliation that would follow.

Iran has shattered all three of these assumptions.

Detection and Tracking: Iran has deployed radar, optical, and signals intelligence systems along the coast of the Strait of Hormuz. al-dhafra.tx:
🇷🇺|RUSSIA IS EVACUATING ITS PERSONNEL. THIS IS MOST SIGNIFICANT PIECE OF NEWS TODAY.

Date is 24 October 2026. Russian diplomats have been instructed to prepare for evacuation from Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain, with orders to be ready within hours. Russian Air Force Tu-134, aircraft type specifically designated for evacuation of high ranking officials, has taken off from Iran. Destination remains undisclosed.

Moscow does not initiate evacuations without cause. Such move implies they have received intelligence suggesting that major event is imminent in coming days. Furthermore, use of Tu-134 to extract personnel from Iran indicates that Moscow deems even Iranian territory unsafe.

This development serves as context for everything else happening today. Keep this at forefront as we examine events unfolding below.

The skies over Saudi Arabia can no longer be secured.

Riyadh reports two powerful explosions. Saudi Civil Defense had issued aerial threat warning just before blasts. Jeddah reports explosions; cause and extent of damage remain undisclosed. Dammam reports flight operations at King Fahd International Airport have been suspended.

India Akasa Air has suspended all flights to and from Riyadh until 30 November 2026. This is no mere temporary adjustment. This is airline voting with own capital: skies over Riyadh are unsafe, so they are ceasing operations for over month.

Saudi airports are appearing on suspended operations list one after another. Saudi Civil Defense is issuing warnings ahead of explosions. Sirens are sounding in Saudi capital.

And what is Saudi Arabia response. It continues to bomb Yemen.

What did Saudi Arabia bomb today.

Four airstrikes hit Harf Sufyan district of Amran Governorate. Two hit Khayar area of Bani Sarim district. Three hit Taiziyah district of Taiz. Four hit across Sahar and Majz districts of Saada. Another four hit Al-Salem area of Saada. In Al-Munqam village of Al-Durayhimi district in Hodeidah, civilian farm was struck, resulting in death of several livestock. Al-Mokha port received one to three strikes. Nihm District, Sanaa received series of airstrikes, resulting in 12 casualties, dead and wounded. Harad District, Hajjah received one strike. Shada border district, Saada received artillery shelling. East of Saada city received missile attack.

In Al-Aqrudh, Al-Misrakh District, Taiz, home of Khalid Abdu Hassan was struck. Woman and two children were killed. Six others were wounded.

This is what Saudi Arabia did on very same day that airports remained closed, capital was under bombardment, and airlines had been grounded for over month. It bombed livestock on farm. It bombed port. It bombed water utility building. It bombed family.

Army that cannot win on battlefield is left with nothing but to bomb such targets. This is not strategy. This is incompetence, incompetence masked by blood of Yemeni people.

Lahj: Path to Aden opens up.

Ansarallah has seized Harir and Al-Nabik defensive lines on Lahj front, advancing toward Shateen Valley. Forces are currently clearing high ground that leads toward Aden.

This is not mere harassment. This is advance. Lahj serves as northern gateway to Aden, with Harir and Al-Nabik acting as its key defensive anchors. With these anchors removed, road to Aden lies open.

Today, Saudi backed forces in Aden were struck by drones, coinciding with collapse of defensive lines in Lahj.

Saudi Arabia entire ground presence in southern Yemen is being squeezed from north.

Iran: Fighter jets scramble; F-35 issues distress signal.

Iranian fighter jets have been conducting intensive flights over coastal waters near Strait of Hormuz.

diego-garcia.tx:
BREAKING 
Chagossians could be handed a veto to stop the islands being handed to Mauritius under a Bill passed by peers this lunchtime.
The British Sovereignty Protection (Chagos Islands) Bill - which cleared the second reading stage in the House of Lords today - would give Chagossians a veto over any deal.
The new law would mean that sovereignty transfers require a referendum of Chagossians and approval by the islands' own government.
The Bill will now go forward to the committee stage when it would need Government support to continue. 
It potentially gives a way-out for Andy Burnham if he wants to drop the deal which has been attacked by US President Donald Trump.
The Chagossian diaspora is thought to be overwhelmingly against the deal. 
Four Chagossoians settled on the archaepelago earlier this year to protest at the Government's plans to hand sovereignty to Mauritius. 
Speaking before the vote, a Foreign Office spokesman told @GBNEWS: “Securing the long-term operation of Diego Garcia remains a top priority for the Government, and protecting the base is the very reason for the agreement with Mauritius.
“We will continue to work with the US and Mauritius to find a way forward that is in the UK's best interests and protects our national security.”

BREAKING: Two men have been re-arrested in connection to activity that took place close to RAF Fairford.

A 24-year-old UK national, and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, were re-arrested on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service.

fairford.tx:
Three weeks ago I wrote that Fairford was most likely an Iranian operation, and that it was probably designed to be stopped. 

Fairford was important to the US war effort against Iran. B-1s and B-52s had been flying strike missions from there since March. It was one of only two bases in Europe they could use, because Spain, France, Italy and Germany had all refused. In July the IRGC publicly named it a legitimate target.

For Iran this was an efficient way to apply pressure. A successful attack that destroyed US aircraft or killed US personnel would have invited a military response. A plot that is stopped short of the wire carries almost no risk. The men involved are British, hired locally and expendable, and Iran can deny any connection, which it has done. No Iranian officers were exposed, and the cost was a few vans, some petrol and whatever the men were paid. The message still got through: keep letting US bombers fly from here, and this is what you can expect. After the IRGC’s public threat in July, there was no doubt who was sending it.

Today two of the men were re-arrested under the National Security Act on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service. Police have confirmed the country is Iran, say state involvement is “highly likely,” and are examining “the ambition behind it.”

The evidence points to this being a warning rather than a serious attempt at sabotage. The vans carried petrol but no explosives, and the men were stopped short of the perimeter. The Telegraph reports that Israeli intelligence had warned MI5 of an imminent Iranian-backed attack on the base, which would explain why the police seemed to be expecting them.

A week later every US bomber had left Fairford. Iran got what it wanted, at almost no cost.

RAF Fairford update from @TerrorismPolice:

This morning two men have been charged under the National Security Act, following an extensive investigation into activity which took place near RAF Fairford on Sunday 27 September.

Head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said:

“Earlier this morning, Nouman Essghir, 24, a British national from the Borough of Westminster, London, was charged under Section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, for suspected activity on Saturday 22 August. He was first arrested at the scene in Gloucestershire on Sunday 27 September, and re-arrested on 20 October. 

“Essghir will appear at Westminster Magistrates Court this morning. 

“A second man, a 25-year-old dual UK/Iranian national, re-arrested on the same date, has been released without charge. However, he remains on police bail following his first arrest on Thursday 1 October. 

“Following the re-arrest of these individuals, detectives also interviewed a further man under caution. 

“As a result, Mohammed Abdul Karim, a 24-year-old British national, from the Borough of Westminster, London, has been charged under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, which makes it an offence to assist a foreign intelligence service.

“In this case, we believe that country to be Iran. Karim will appear at Westminster Magistrates today. 

“The five other men arrested in connection with this investigation, remain on police bail. 

“We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state, and as the Director General of Mi5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat. 

“The public can help us with this, and as always, I would urge them to report anything that they’re worried about – those reports can and do make a difference.”

Many Religions in America, but One Stands Out as a Problem.

There are approximately 3 million Hindus, 4 million Buddhists, and 8 million Jews in America.

Since 1994, I have not found a documented terrorist attack motivated by Hinduism or Buddhism that killed Americans on U.S. soil.

I found two cases involving suspected Jewish extremists: the 1994 bombings targeting Jewish organizations that supported peace with Palestinians, and a 2001 conspiracy to bomb a mosque that was stopped before it could be carried out.

Now compare that with Islam.

There are approximately 4 million Muslims in America, roughly the same number as Buddhists and half the Jewish population.

Yet since 1994, Muslim terrorists have murdered thousands of Americans on American soil. The September 11 attacks alone killed nearly 3,000 people. The Fort Hood shooter murdered 13. The Orlando nightclub shooter murdered 49. The San Bernardino terrorists murdered 14.

These were not isolated incidents. Islamic terrorist attacks and plots have involved people from different countries, ethnic backgrounds, and nationalities, including converts to Islam.

What did these terrorists have in common?

They invoked Islam to justify their violence.

And yet, after every attack, we hear the same predictable explanation: They misunderstood Islam! They misinterpreted the Quran! They don’t represent the religion!

Really?

Then answer one simple question.

Why does this particular pattern of religiously justified terrorism repeatedly emerge from Islam, while we do not see anything comparable from Hinduism or Buddhism in America?

Are we supposed to believe that generations of jihadists, from different countries, speaking different languages, and living in different cultures, all independently misunderstood the same religion in exactly the same violent direction?

And that their misunderstanding somehow repeatedly led them to the same objectives: jihad, Islamic supremacy, and the establishment of Sharia?

At what point do we stop treating the ideology as an innocent bystander?

Muslims preachers and activists openly seek to replace secular government with sharia. That is not a conspiracy theory. It is a political and theological objective they themselves proclaim.

Of course, not every Muslim supports terrorism or wants Sharia imposed on America. But that fact does not erase the ideology motivating those who do.

The question is not whether every Muslim is a terrorist. The question is why so many Muslim terrorists have justified their actions through the same religious texts and doctrines.

You cannot keep blaming every terrorist attack on a misunderstanding while refusing to examine what is being understood.

It is clear that Islam stands apart from other religions in America as a source of serious dangers that have cost American lives and continue to threaten the safety and foundations of our society.

Big week of @TheUFL meetings on both the business and football operations sides as we prepare for 2027.

As promised, the UFL will be TRANSPARENT. On AND off the field!!!!

Today, our team presented stadium availability for all eight UFL teams. Seven venues offered significant flexibility. Unfortunately, St. Louis was the exception.

Based on the BattleDome dates currently available, the @BattlehawksUFL would play FOUR straight home games, followed by FIVE consecutive road games, and potentially return home for Week 10.

FOUR HOME GAMES. FIVE ROAD GAMES.

Sorry, but that just DOESN’T WORK FOR US!!!!

This isn’t your old spring football league. We’re going to do things DIFFERENTLY!!!! That means better planning, better partnerships, more marketing, more transparency, and most importantly, putting our FANS FIRST!!!!

St. Louis has one of the most passionate fan bases in football. These fans arrive early, stay late, and travel to support their team. I experienced it firsthand at the BattleDome and watching Battlehawks fans travel to Louisville.

I promised St. Louis we would do more, starting with bringing the UFL Draft to St. Louis on November 18.

But promises mean nothing without a

fort-hood.tx:
@RepoleStable Appreciate the transparency and the invitation for ideas. Here’s a practical way to keep the Battlehawks at the Dome while fixing the 4-home / 5-road stretch and doing right by St. Louis fans:

Finish training camp in Arlington, then base the Battlehawks in St. Louis for the first five weeks of the season. Secure short-term player and staff housing so the team is fully embedded in the market. Front-load their first four home games at the BattleDome during that window, then play their fifth “home” game at Fort Leonard Wood as a Hats Off to Heroes military appreciation game for the troops! similar to the historic Fort Hood game the league hosted last year. Fort Leonard Wood is only a couple hours from St. Louis, so it still functions as a regional home date while giving the team a meaningful way to honor service members.

During the five-week residency, lean into local presence: open practices, community events, youth clinics, season-ticket member dinners, and player appearances. Use the stretch as a concentrated marketing push to drive early ticket sales and re-energize the market. Film a short documentary series following the team’s time in St. Louis and the Fort Leonard Wood game, great content that highlights both the fan base and the league’s military outreach.

After the five weeks, return to the hub. Slot one game around Week 7 or 8 in Dallas so the remaining road stretch isn’t five straight. Other teams travel weekly anyway, so the early clustered homes still give St. Louis a strong start (they’ve already had an extra home game in recent years). The temporary residency and military game more than offset the schedule compression by creating real local access, energy, and goodwill.

This also works as a low-risk pilot. The hub model saves money, but it limits true market presence and season-ticket engagement. Testing a short “home residency” with one team, plus a regional military date, could inform how the league handles future scheduling or market development without abandoning the centralized model.

St. Louis fans have shown they’ll show up and travel. Giving them a concentrated, high-visibility home stretch, plus a special game for the troops nearby, turns a tough schedule constrain into something that feels intentional and fan-focused. Worth exploring.

pearl-harbor.t: The best Japanese airplane of WW2 was the Mitsubishi A6M Zero. For about a year and a half, it owned the skies over the Pacific. Then one crash on a tiny Alask…
pearl-harbor.tx:
The best Japanese airplane of WW2 was the Mitsubishi A6M Zero. For about a year and a half, it owned the skies over the Pacific. Then one crash on a tiny Alaskan island helped end its reign.

The Japanese Navy asked for the impossible in 1937. A carrier fighter that could outclimb, outturn, and outrange anything in the world. Most engineers said you couldn't get all of that in one plane.

A designer named Jiro Horikoshi did it by cutting weight everywhere. Thin aluminum skin. A lightweight frame with holes drilled into the parts to shave off ounces. No armor plate behind the pilot. No self-sealing fuel tanks. Every pound saved went into speed, agility, and fuel.

The Navy accepted it in 1940, the year 2600 on the Japanese imperial calendar. Type 0. The Zero.

It made its combat debut over China that September. A small group of Zeros tore apart a much larger formation of Chinese fighters without losing a single plane.

An American named Claire Chennault, advising the Chinese, sent warnings home about this new Japanese fighter. They were largely ignored. American officials didn't believe Japan could build something that good.

Then came December 1941.

Zeros escorted the attack on Pearl Harbor. In the months that followed, they swept across the Philippines, Malaya, the Dutch East Indies, and the Indian Ocean. With a drop tank, the Zero could fly well over a thousand miles, so far that Allied pilots sometimes assumed there must be a secret carrier nearby. In a turning dogfight, almost nothing could stay with it.

American and British pilots got a simple instruction: don't dogfight a Zero.

Then, on June 4, 1942, during a raid on Dutch Harbor in the Aleutian Islands, a young Japanese pilot named Tadayoshi Koga had his Zero's oil line hit by ground fire.

He headed for the remote island of Akutan to make an emergency landing. From above, the flat ground looked solid. It was a bog. His wheels dug in, the Zero flipped onto its back, and Koga was killed instantly.

The plane, though, was almost intact.

A month later, a US Navy patrol plane spotted the wreck. The Zero was hauled out, shipped to San Diego, repaired, and test-flown by American pilots. For the first time, the US could study the Zero in the air.

The tests revealed the weaknesses behind the legend. At high speeds, the Zero's controls stiffened and it couldn't roll fast. Its engine could cut out briefly when it pushed into a steep dive. And with no armor and no self-sealing tanks, it couldn't take punishment.

American pilots learned to stop turning with it. They used speed, dove away, and attacked in pairs with tactics like the Thach Weave. A few good hits and the Zero went down in flames.

And in 1943, the F6F Hellcat arrived. Faster, tougher, better armed. By 1944, Zeros were falling in huge numbers, many flown by rookies replacing the veterans already lost.

In the war's final months, Zeros were loaded with bombs and flown as kamikazes.

Japan built more than 10,000 of them, more than any other Japanese aircraft. Horikoshi lived to see his creation turned into a suicide weapon. He wrote about how much the waste of young men's lives troubled him.

The Zero didn't lose because it was a bad plane. It lost because it was built for a short war. And Japan didn't get one.

pearl-harbor.t: The best Japanese ship class of WW2 was the Shokaku class. Only two ships were ever built. Between them, they fought in almost every major carrier battle of th…
pearl-harbor.tx:
The best Japanese ship class of WW2 was the Shokaku class. Only two ships were ever built. Between them, they fought in almost every major carrier battle of the Pacific War.

Their names were Shokaku, "Soaring Crane," and Zuikaku, "Auspicious Crane."

In 1936, Japan walked away from the naval treaties that had limited the size of its fleet. For the first time in years, Japanese designers could build exactly the carrier they wanted. Everything they had learned went into these two ships.

They were big, fast, and well protected, and they could carry more than 70 aircraft each. When they joined the fleet in the late summer and fall of 1941, they were arguably the best aircraft carriers in the world.

They were commissioned just a few months before Pearl Harbor.

On December 7, 1941, both sailed with the strike force. Their crews were the newest and least experienced in the fleet, so their planes were sent mostly against the airfields on Oahu.

Months later, they took part in the Japanese raid into the Indian Ocean that sank a British carrier and several warships.

Then came Coral Sea in May 1942. The first carrier battle in history, where the opposing fleets never saw each other. Planes from Shokaku and Zuikaku helped sink USS Lexington. But Shokaku was hit by bombs and badly damaged. Zuikaku came through unhurt but lost a large share of its aircraft and pilots.

So neither ship was at Midway a month later.

Historians still argue about what might have happened if those two extra carriers had been there. Instead, Japan lost four carriers in a single day. Shokaku and Zuikaku became the heart of what was left.

In August 1942, at the Eastern Solomons, their planes damaged USS Enterprise. In October 1942, at Santa Cruz, they helped sink USS Hornet, the carrier that had launched the Doolittle Raid. It was the last American fleet carrier sunk in the entire war.

Shokaku took a beating at Santa Cruz too. Bombs wrecked her flight deck. She survived. Again.

But by 1944, the war had turned. The veteran pilots who had flown at Pearl Harbor were mostly dead. The Essex-class carriers were arriving in waves.

On June 19, 1944, during the Battle of the Philippine Sea, the American submarine USS Cavalla slipped in close and put torpedoes into Shokaku. Fuel vapor spread through the ship. A few hours later she blew up and sank. More than 1,200 men went down with her.

Zuikaku was now the last of the six carriers that had attacked Pearl Harbor.

In October 1944, at Leyte Gulf, Japan had planes but almost no trained pilots left to fly them. So Zuikaku was given one final mission: be the bait. Sail north, get spotted, and lure Halsey's fleet away from the landing beaches.

It worked. Halsey charged north with everything he had.

On October 25, off Cape Engaño, wave after wave of American planes hit Zuikaku. As she began to roll over, her crew gathered on the tilted flight deck and lowered the flag. Someone photographed them saluting it. Then she sank.

Zuikaku fought in five of the six great carrier battles of the Pacific War. Midway was the only one she missed.

The two cranes were there at the very beginning. And one of them was there at the very end.

pearl-harbor.t: Three days after Pearl Harbor, someone took a saw to the cherry trees in Washington. Four trees came down. One stump had an angry message carved into it. Lette…
pearl-harbor.tx:
Three days after Pearl Harbor, someone took a saw to the cherry trees in Washington.

Four trees came down. One stump had an angry message carved into it.

Letters poured in demanding the rest be torn out by the roots.

Those trees were a gift from Tokyo. America was now at war with Tokyo.

So Washington made a quiet decision.

They gave the trees a new name. "Oriental" cherry trees.

Not to erase them. To protect them.

It worked. The trees made it through the war.

Then, in 1952, Tokyo had a problem. The riverbank where those trees were born, along the Arakawa River, had withered away during the war.

Tokyo asked America for help.

America sent cuttings from the Washington trees. Back home. To the exact riverbank they came from.

And again in 1981.

Today, that riverbank is lined with cherry trees for nearly three miles. Every April, Tokyo families spread their picnic blankets under them.

My father has gone every spring for 40 years.

Last night I told him where his trees came from.

He was quiet for a while. Then he said, "So they were holding them for us."

America, you could have cut them all down.

You kept them safe instead.

Then you sent them home.

pearl-harbor.t: On December 7, 1941, Doris “Dorie” Miller was doing his duty aboard the USS West Virginia when Pearl Harbor came under attack. 🇺🇸 Miller was a Black sailor in…
pearl-harbor.tx:
On December 7, 1941, Doris “Dorie” Miller was doing his duty aboard the USS West Virginia when Pearl Harbor came under attack. 🇺🇸

Miller was a Black sailor in a Navy that had assigned him to mess duty. He had never been trained to operate the ship’s antiaircraft guns.

Then the bombs began falling.

Miller helped move his wounded captain to safety. With the ship under fire, he climbed to a machine gun and kept firing until the ammunition was gone. Afterward, he helped carry wounded sailors to safety.

He didn’t stop to ask whether he was trained for the moment or whether anyone would remember his name. He saw people in danger—and he stepped forward. 🫡

In 1942, Miller became the first Black sailor to receive the Navy Cross for his courage at Pearl Harbor.

His story is a reminder that a hero isn’t always the person given the spotlight or the right opportunities. Sometimes it’s the person who rises to the moment when everyone else needs him.

Dorie Miller did. 💙

pearl-harbor.t: Oct 25, 1944. Admiral Halsey wins a crushing victory. And it's the most controversial decision of his career. Japan's plan at Leyte Gulf depended on a decoy. A…
pearl-harbor.tx:
Oct 25, 1944. Admiral Halsey wins a crushing victory. And it's the most controversial decision of his career.

Japan's plan at Leyte Gulf depended on a decoy.

Admiral Jisaburo Ozawa sailed south from Japan with four aircraft carriers, including Zuikaku, the last surviving carrier of the six that had attacked Pearl Harbor. But the carriers had almost no planes left aboard. Japan had lost too many pilots. Ozawa's job was to be seen, and to pull Halsey's fleet away from Leyte.

On the afternoon of Oct 24, American scouts found him.

Halsey believed Kurita's Center Force had been beaten in the Sibuyan Sea. The carriers looked like the real threat. That night, he took his entire fleet north. Every carrier and every fast battleship. He left nothing guarding San Bernardino Strait.

Back at Leyte, Admiral Kinkaid and others believed a battleship force, Task Force 34, had been left behind to guard the strait. It hadn't.

The next morning, Halsey's planes tore into Ozawa's fleet. Wave after wave. The light carrier Chitose sank. Then Zuiho. Then Zuikaku, the last of the Pearl Harbor carriers, rolled over and went down. By the end of the battle, all four Japanese carriers were gone.

But far to the south, Kurita's battleships were attacking Taffy 3 off Samar. Frantic calls for help went out.

At about 10 a.m., Halsey got a message from Admiral Nimitz at Pearl Harbor. It asked where Task Force 34 was.

To confuse Japanese codebreakers, radio operators added nonsense phrases to the start and end of messages. The decoders on Halsey's flagship cut off the opening padding but left the end. So the message Halsey read ended with the words "the world wonders."

Halsey took it as a public insult from his commander. He was reportedly furious.

He finally sent his battleships south. They had been close to finishing off Ozawa's surviving ships. By the time they reached San Bernardino Strait, Kurita was already gone.

Halsey had destroyed Japan's carrier force. But he had taken the bait, left the beachhead open, and spent the rest of his life defending the decision.

pearl-harbor.tx:
Blessings on Red Friday: 🙏❤️

With the American Pacific Fleet shifted on President Franklin Roosevelt’s orders from San Diego to the base at Pearl Harbor, near Honolulu, Hawaii, Kidd watched and prepared for conflict in 1941. He had spent 39 years in the US Navy. At the same time, he could witness the development of his son, Isaac C. Kidd Jr., who, following his father’s footsteps, graduated from Annapolis in 1941.

Rear Admiral Kidd was on the Arizona when waves of Japanese planes descended on Pearl Harbor shortly before 8:00 a.m. on Sunday, December 7, 1941. One of eight battleships on “Battleship Row” moored next to Ford Island, the old vessel made an inviting target for enemy pilots. Despite the terrors all around him, Kidd did not waver, though, from fulfilling his duties. As Senior Officer Present Afloat, he manned the bridge with the ship’s captain, Franklin Van Valkenburgh. Kidd’s Medal of Honor citation noted “his conspicuous devotion to duty, extraordinary courage, and complete disregard of his own life.” 

Japanese aircraft steadily unleashed devastation and death on the Arizona. At 8:06 a.m., a massive armor-piercing bomb penetrated the decks beside the front turrets. Arizona’s forward magazines ignited. A huge explosion rocked the battleship, lifting it out of the water.

According to the Navy’s documentation, Rear Admiral Kidd was killed when a Japanese bomb landed directly on the bridge. Just 57 years old, he was the first Flag Officer of the US Navy to die in World War II and, in fact, the first ever to lose his life fighting a foreign adversary. Captain Van Valkenburgh would also not survive the attack. 

At 9:00 a.m., Lieutenant Commander Samuel Fuqua, unable to find Kidd or Van Valkenburgh, ordered Arizona’s crew to evacuate. Some 330–350 sailors and Marines escaped the doomed battleship. For his leadership in this dreadful moment, Fuqua received the Medal of Honor.
Rear Admiral Isaac C. Kidd was among the 1,177 men who perished on the USS Arizona. His remains were never recovered. Remarkably, however, Navy divers discovered Kidd’s Naval Academy class ring fused to the bulkhead in the ship’s conning tower.

The National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific lists Kidd’s name on its Wall of the Missing. As one of the 10 posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor for what they did at Pearl Harbor (so, too, was Captain Van Valkenburgh), Kidd’s sacrifice has not at all been forgotten. The Navy has named three destroyers after him—the first christened by his wife Inez in 1943 (which has been the centerpiece of the USS Kidd memorial in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, since 1983), the most recent in 2007—and dedicated to him the Rear Admiral Isaac C. Kidd Computer Center in Bratenahl, in his home state of Ohio.

yokosuka.t: For seventy years after World War II, the law was one-sided: if an enemy attacked Japan, American sailors were sworn to die defending her, but if an American s…
yokosuka.tx:
For seventy years after World War II, the law was one-sided: if an enemy attacked Japan, American sailors were sworn to die defending her, but if an American ship was attacked right next to a Japanese warship, Japanese sailors were legally forbidden to defend their American friends.

Prime Minister Shinzo Abe refused to accept that shame any longer.

Despite screaming protesters outside the parliament building in Tokyo, Abe passed historic security laws so Japan could finally stand shoulder to shoulder with the United States.

On May 1, 2017, as North Korea threatened missile strikes across the Pacific, that promise became steel on the water.

Why did Japan send its largest warship, the 814-foot helicopter destroyer JS Izumo, to guard the U.S. Navy ship USNS Richard E. Byrd? Because the Byrd was a vital ammunition and cargo supply vessel crewed mostly by American civilian mariners, steaming south from Yokosuka to resupply the USS Carl Vinson carrier strike group.

Without heavily armed escorts, a supply ship is the most vulnerable target at sea.

As the American supply ship cleared Tokyo Bay, the massive gray flat-top JS Izumo pulled alongside her port beam, launching SH-60K anti-submarine helicopters overhead to sweep the waters all the way to Shikoku.

American sailors watching from the bridge knew what they were seeing. For the first time in postwar history, the Rising Sun flag was sailing as an armed bodyguard for the Stars and Stripes.

A true friend does not hide behind your shield forever. One day, he steps up and locks his shield with yours.

yokosuka.t: Critics love to say that twenty-year-old American Marines on New Year's Eve liberty in Japan only care about partying. On December 31, 2016, four young U.S. Ma…
yokosuka.tx:
Critics love to say that twenty-year-old American Marines on New Year's Eve liberty in Japan only care about partying.

On December 31, 2016, four young U.S. Marines were walking in Yokosuka when an SUV plunged five stories off a garage.

The vehicle slammed upside down onto the pavement with a Japanese family of five inside. Eight local bystanders and two U.S. Navy Sailors pulled on the doors, but the crushed roof jammed the steel shut.

Waiting ten minutes for hydraulic rescue jaws meant the children trapped upside down inside the compressed cabin would suffocate or bleed out.

Marine Lance Corporal James Flores shouted that they had to flip the heavy vehicle upright by hand, and Lance Corporal Raheem Gilliam used the Japanese numbers he had just practiced in his barracks to unite the crowd.

"Ichi, ni, san!" Gilliam roared.

Four Marines, two Sailors, and eight Japanese citizens locked their fingers under the twisted frame and deadlifted the SUV upright in one heave.

The Marines crawled into the glass, pulled two young Japanese boys out alive, and used their Combat Lifesaver training to stop the bleeding until ambulances arrived.

Walking to the emergency room afterward to get his own cut hands checked, Gilliam did not brag. He quietly called Oklahoma just to tell his mother he loved her.

Honor needs no translator when good men lift together.

yokosuka.t: On September 21, 2001, while smoke was still rising from the rubble of the World Trade Center in New York, the aircraft carrier USS Kitty Hawk prepared to sail…
yokosuka.tx:
On September 21, 2001, while smoke was still rising from the rubble of the World Trade Center in New York, the aircraft carrier USS Kitty Hawk prepared to sail out of Yokosuka, Japan, into war.

Every sailor on board knew the danger they faced before even reaching the open ocean.

Why was leaving Tokyo Bay the most dangerous moment of the voyage? Because to reach the Pacific, the giant carrier had to squeeze through the narrow Uraga Channel, a crowded waterway packed with hundreds of small civilian boats where a single suicide vessel loaded with explosives could strike at point-blank range.

As the Kitty Hawk slipped her moorings that morning, the American crew looked out from the flight deck in stunned silence.

Gray destroyers of the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force and white patrol boats of the Japan Coast Guard had formed a tight steel wall directly along both sides of the American carrier.

The Japanese captains positioned their own hulls between the USS Kitty Hawk and all oncoming boat traffic. If a terrorist boat tried to ram the American carrier, it would have to hit a Japanese ship first.

Then the American sailors looked at the rocky cliffs of Yokosuka and Kannonzaki Lighthouse.

Thousands of Japanese citizens, base workers, and families were standing shoulder to shoulder along the shore, waving American flags and holding up hand-painted banners that read "We Are With You."

In her hour of deepest grief, America did not sail out of Japan alone. Japan sailed as her shield.

yokosuka.t: Every American sailor stationed in Yokosuka knows what happened on the night of June 17, 2017, even if American television quickly moved on. At 1:30 AM in pitc…
yokosuka.tx:
Every American sailor stationed in Yokosuka knows what happened on the night of June 17, 2017, even if American television quickly moved on.

At 1:30 AM in pitch darkness off the Izu Peninsula, a thirty-thousand-ton container ship tore a massive gash straight into the starboard side of the U.S. Navy destroyer USS Fitzgerald.

Freezing black ocean water flooded the berthing compartments in seconds. Seven American sailors gave their lives in the dark while their shipmates fought with bare hands and wrenches to seal the hatches and keep the warship from sinking.

Why could the destroyer not simply call U.S. Navy helicopters on its own? Because the impact had crushed the captain's cabin and knocked out most of the ship's primary radio communications, leaving her listing in the dark sea.

Before dawn broke, white hulls with blue stripes and gray Japanese rotors appeared through the mist.

Ships from the Japan Coast Guard and a Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force SH-60K helicopter arrived first on the scene.

Hovering over the tilting steel deck in heavy wind, a Japanese Navy helicopter crew lowered a rescue litter and hoisted Fitzgerald's critically injured commanding officer, Commander Bryce Benson, and two wounded sailors straight to the U.S. Naval Hospital in Yokosuka.

Then Japanese harbor tugboats locked onto the wounded American destroyer and guided her inch by inch all the way back to port so she would not sink.

When the ship finally reached Yokosuka at 6:15 PM, Japanese crewmen stood on their decks and saluted in silence.

You find out who your true brothers are at two in the morning when the water is rising.

NEW: U.S. Forces Japan will ban all BYD vehicles from Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, citing security risks. 

The ban applies with no exceptions to personnel’s private cars, contractor vehicles, taxis and delivery vans, with security forces turning them away at every gate. 

Kadena, the largest U.S. Air Force base overseas, hosts the 18th Wing and the Typhon missile system capable of launching Tomahawk cruise missiles. 

Base spokesperson Lt. Col. Alli Stormer said the vehicles “present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” without giving details. 

Yonhap, citing U.S. military officials, said the concern is that cameras, sensors, GPS and connected features could collect and leak sensitive information.

kadena.t: How low can an F-22 fly before the climb becomes the real test? At Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, the Raptor’s low departure offers a rare look at the aircraft’s…
kadena.tx:
How low can an F-22 fly before the climb becomes the real test?

At Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, the Raptor’s low departure offers a rare look at the aircraft’s proportions and power before it banks into the clouds.

Its twin F119 engines provide the thrust for rapid acceleration, while its carefully shaped airframe reduces radar visibility. But stealth is only one part of the design. The F-22 combines low-observable shaping with supercruise capability and thrust vectoring, giving it a balance of speed, agility and survivability.

The striking part is how quickly this angular aircraft transitions from a low runway pass to a climb into the sky.

qt.t: OBAMA: Iran didn't have nuclear weapons because I had put a deal in place and I didn't have to fire a missile to do it. I just had to engage in diplomacy.

fordow.tx:
If anyone believes this nonsense, here are the facts he is counting on you not knowing.

The deal did not end Iran's nuclear program. It rented a pause. Iran kept its centrifuges, kept Fordow buried in a mountain, kept enriching to 3.67%, and the key restrictions came with expiration dates. The sunset clauses began lifting in 2025. Obama's own answer at the time was that breakout time "would have shrunk almost down to zero" as the deal expired. His deal scheduled the problem for his successors.

The regime lied its way into the deal. The JCPOA was premised on Iran coming clean about past weapons work. In 2018 Israel pulled Iran's own nuclear archive out of a Tehran warehouse: tens of thousands of documents on the Amad Project, a crash program to build nuclear weapons, preserved and hidden while Iran certified it had no such program. The IAEA later found uranium traces at undeclared sites Iran never explained.

The deal paid for terror. Sanctions relief unfroze roughly $100 billion and the US delivered $1.7 billion in cash. That money flowed to the IRGC, Hezbollah, Hamas, and the Houthis. Diplomacy with a regime at war with you is financing, not peace.

And the result? By 2025 Iran was enriching to 60%, a short technical step from weapons grade, with enough material for multiple bombs and the IAEA declaring it in violation of its obligations. Hidden beneath a mountain, Iran’s Fordow nuclear facility was designed to withstand conventional airstrikes. Then came the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator—the US military’s 30,000-pound bunker-buster, engineered to strike deeply buried and heavily fortified targets.

natanz.tx:
As Midterms and Israeli elections loom on the horizon, there is a growing feeling that we are currently on the eve of another large-scale military campaign against Iran.

Several indicators are pointing to the resumption of large-scale combat operations by the United States and Israel in Iran in the near future:

1) On October 21, NBC News reported, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, that the US military has quietly been scaling back its troop presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, while the State Department has ordered a further reduction in staff at multiple diplomatic posts in the region. One of the sources said that the withdrawal of American forces and diplomatic personnel is similar to drawdowns at bases and embassies that the Pentagon and State Department initiated before the beginning of the war with Iran back in February.

2) Earlier this week, Israeli Air Force conducted a long-range sortie through the Syrian and Iraqi airspace toward Iranian border, consistent with the profile of simulated strike against Iran. The exercise involved dozens of fighter jets and numerous refueling aircraft. According to Axios, some U.S. sources said they had the impression that Israel was hoping the Iranians would fire at the aircraft, providing a justification for launching strikes against Tehran. 

3) In mid-October, Axios also reported that US President Trump and Israeli PM Netanyahu discussed the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, according to two American officials, one Israeli official and a fourth source with knowledge of the matter. An Israeli official said Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward resuming attacks, but then grew more hesitant, but another source said Israeli and U.S. militaries remained on alert and concluding preparations to be ready in case he changes his mind.

4) Anticipating the renewed attack by the US and Israel, Iran has began fortifying its defenses, rallying loyalists and threatening a wider, harsher response against Washington and its Gulf allies, according to WSJ story from mid-October. The outlet also wrote that the Iranians have reinforced protection around its nuclear sites and other security-related bunkers. The efforts included construction of passive defense measures such as makeshift dirt mounds around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear sites to impede any attempted raid by ground forces.

5) On October 19, the Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel, where he met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Ovda Air Base. The meeting also included Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz. IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir and other senior Israeli officials were reportedly not invited, for confidentiality reasons. Hegseth arrived via military transport rather than a standard US government aircraft to keep the trip low-profile. 

The new military operation against Iran might involve intense strikes targeting nuclear sites, energy infrastructure, and missile/drone arsenals as a way to force Tehran to accepting terms it has so far resisted after nearly eight months of conflict, sanctions, and the US naval blockade. Iran has refused to move enriched uranium abroad or make nuclear concessions, and it has used leverage over the Strait of Hormuz. 

It's also noting that the Iranian economy suffered severe strain due to US naval blockade of Iranian ports and intensified sanctions. Oil exports have largely collapsed, while the inflation remains extremely high. The renewed bombing campaign against energy and economic targets could be a factor that pushes the Iranian economy "over the brink" and forces the regime to make concessions.

Multiple Russian Il-76 military cargo planes landed at Bushehr Air Base in southern Iran a few hours ago, per local sources.

Here's what's happening:

→ FULL EVACUATION: The planes came to take every Russian worker out of the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant ahead of a military escalation.

→ WEAPONS ON BOARD: The same sources say the flights are also bringing weapons into Iran.

→ LAST TIME: Russia's nuclear company Rosatom last pulled its staff out on February 28, the day the war started: 94 people in a single day.

→ JUST RETURNED: After the war started, Rosatom took more than 600 staff out, but by mid-October 135 were back on site, with plans for 200.

→ PLAN REVERSED: A few weeks ago, Rosatom's boss said "We are now moving in the opposite direction, returning to the site," and now Russia is FLYING its people out.

Think about this.

Russia spent weeks sending its nuclear staff back to Iran.

And now its military planes have landed to get every one of them out.

This could become one of the biggest warning signs of this war.

Mehrabad airport , Iran’s main airport has been attacked . Numerous explosions seen , no reports on mainstream media . No cause explained and no group taking responsibility. Massive cargo plane with transponder off landed just before explosions occurred.
An Iranian radar site in Tabriz was also destroyed by a drone .

At least 20 vessels ( none Iranian) transited through Hormuz this weekend ( 10 confirmed and estimated 10 unconfirmed as transponders off ) 

Saudi-led forces reportedly carried out airstrikes against Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen over the weekend of 24–25 October 2026. The fighting escalated as the Houthis launched missiles and drones towards Saudi Arabia.
According to reporting by Al Jazeera and other outlets, the weekend saw attacks in both directions. 
Saturday, 24 October: Reports described Saudi-led coalition airstrikes hitting areas controlled by the Houthis in Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa.
Sunday, 25 October: Saudi Arabia's coalition reported intercepting Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Riyadh and southern parts of the kingdom. 
- Casualties: Houthi-run media reported deaths and injuries from the airstrikes, including in Sanaa and Hodeidah. Those figures have not been independently verified. 
The key point: this was not just Saudi Arabia intercepting incoming missiles. Saudi-led forces were also reportedly striking Houthi positions inside Yemen, marking a further escalation

Reported attacks

hodeidah.tx:
🇾🇪|The Fall of Jabal Han: The Last Barrier West of Taiz Vanishes in Ten Minutes

October 20, 2026. Saudi-backed mobilization forces have withdrawn from Jabal Han.

Jabal Han is no ordinary mountain. It is the highest vantage point west of the city of Taiz. Its artillery positions command the main roads leading into the city's western sector, and its observation posts monitor every vehicle entering or leaving Taiz. Its fortifications, reinforced repeatedly over the last decade, were considered the final, impenetrable barrier west of Taiz.

Yet once Ansarallah completed their encirclement, this barrier could not withstand a single decisive offensive.

💥 The Geometry of Encirclement

The fall of Jabal Han was not the result of a direct frontal assault. Ansarallah did not attempt to storm the mountain slopes from the west. Instead, they bypassed it.

First, they seized Al-Murab'ah and the Al-Ariel heights, severing the link between Jabal Han and its rear supply lines. They then tightened the noose, leaving the defenders on the mountain to realize they were no longer holding a defensive position. They had become besieged hostages.

Faced with a choice, to have their soldiers wiped out one by one in their positions or to retreat, the commanders chose to withdraw.

Jabal Han did not fall because it was stormed. It fell because it was bypassed. And the very force that bypassed it now stands atop its summit.

🎯 The Western Flank Opened

Jabal Han lies to the west of Taiz. To its south is the direction of the old airport. To its east, the city's built-up urban area. And to its north, the highway connecting Taiz to Hodeidah.

All three directions now lie within the line of sight of Ansarallah.

The defensive architecture of the Saudi-backed forces in Taiz relies on a network of mutually supporting key heights. Jabal Han served as the linchpin of that western defense. With the key strongpoint removed, the western defensive line is no longer a continuous front. It has been fractured into a series of isolated, disconnected positions.

The fall of Taiz is not merely imminent. It is already underway. Jabal Han is the penultimate node. The final node lies within the city streets themselves.

📜 Who Turned Taiz into a Battlefield?

Taiz has been under siege for years. It is not Ansar Allah that has besieged the city. Rather, it is those who transformed the city into a military stronghold.

They looted shops in the city center and padded their ranks with ghost soldiers. As Ansar Allah advanced, they retreated, abandoning their positions and fleeing to Aden. They released criminals from prisons, rearmed them, and unleashed them back into the city to terrorize the civilian population. They severed vital supply routes, turned the entire city into a military target, and then demanded that civilians take up arms to defend their homes.

The defenders at Jabal Han have retreated. The civilians trapped in the city have nowhere left to go.

⚔️ Saudi Arabia's Calculus

Saudi Arabia has poured funds, weaponry, training, and command coordination into Taiz. In return, it has received nothing but a string of retreats: the old airport, the Al-Hanjar checkpoint, Jabal Han, and every other strongpoint along the western front.

Saudi Arabia's war budget could purchase equipment, but it could not buy men willing to hold the high ground on its behalf.

The defenders at Jabal Han were not wiped out in battle. They were abandoned, forsaken by their commanders, by their political leadership, and by a government that holds meetings in Aden, signs contracts in Riyadh, and appears on television to claim, look at what we are doing.

Long live the people of Taiz. Long live Yemen. Long live Ansar Allah. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

hodeidah.t: 51 Killed and Injured, Including 21 Martyrs, in Five Saudi Attacks Across Yemen Within 24 Hours The death toll from Saudi airstrikes targeting Yemen's capital,…
hodeidah.tx:
51 Killed and Injured, Including 21 Martyrs, in Five Saudi Attacks Across Yemen Within 24 Hours

The death toll from Saudi airstrikes targeting Yemen's capital, Sana'a, and the governorates of Sana'a, Hodeidah, Taiz, and Saada has risen to 21 martyrs and 30 wounded, bringing the total number of casualties to 51, according to updated figures as of Saturday, October 24, 2026.

Details reveal attacks on Yemeni families inside their homes and workers' residential facilities, with women and children accounting for a large proportion of the victims, including an infant no older than one year. The airstrikes also targeted a shelter for African migrants, while several families lost multiple members in the attacks.

Sana'a Capital: 3 Martyrs and 2 Wounded

Saudi enemy warplanes targeted the home of Fuad Sharaf Al-Shaabi in the Asr area, west of Sana'a, killing three members of the same family.

The martyrs were 10-year-old Omaima Fuad Sharaf Al-Shaabi, her 16-year-old brother Louay, and their 26-year-old uncle Ali Sharaf Al-Shaabi.

The children's mother, Zainab Hifzallah Mujahid, and her brother Amer Hifzallah Mujahid were also wounded. Amer's condition was described as critical. The Saudi attack turned the family's home into a scene of death and destruction.

Sana'a Governorate: 8 Martyrs and 15 Wounded

Detailed casualty reports from the Saudi airstrikes targeting the families of cement factory workers in Hamdan District confirmed eight martyrs and fifteen wounded.

Among those killed were three-year-old Alin Khalil Hizam Awad and six-year-old Ghaida Asaad Abdullah Al-Maqra'i.

The victims also included 30-year-old Aisha Ali Hamoud Al-Maqra'i, who died from suffocation; 18-year-old Hanan Hani Qasim Al-Wasabi; Zainab Khalil Hizam Murshid; Hanadi Saleh Ahmed Awad; Nawal Fuad Al-Ezzi Ali; and Thabit Saeed Humaid Al-Hakimi.

The list of wounded includes seven children aged between one and six years. Among them are one-year-old Nizar Hani Qasim Al-Wasabi, three-year-old Enas Khaled Abdulwahab Abdulqader Al-Osaimi, and her five-year-old sister Esraa.

Six-year-old Areen Osama Hamoud suffered wounds and fractures. Five-year-old Murtada Abdulwahab, three-year-old Muneeb Ibrahim Hassan Haidar, and five-year-old Mila Ibrahim Hassan Haidar were also injured.

The wounded also include eight adults, among them 35-year-old Saadia Ali Futayni Qasim, who sustained serious injuries.

These details show that the airstrikes targeted residential facilities housing several working families struggling to earn a dignified living amid the severe humanitarian conditions caused by the Saudi blockade.

Hodeidah Governorate: 5 Martyrs and 1 Wounded

Saudi enemy warplanes targeted the home of Abdulwahed Al-Wasabi in Al-Tuhayta District.

The attack killed Al-Wasabi, his two wives, and two of his children, while his third daughter was wounded.

The family lost five members in a single airstrike, illustrating the devastating consequences of Saudi attacks on civilians inside their homes.

Taiz Governorate: 4 Martyrs and 5 Wounded

Saudi airstrikes targeted the home of Khaled Abdu Saeed Hassan in Hiba village, Al-Aqrood area, Al-Misrakh District, killing four members of the same family and wounding five others.

The Taiz Governorate Health and Environment Office confirmed that all four martyrs were women and children.

They were 35-year-old Nabiha Sharaf Hassan Naji, 10-year-old Bayna Khaled Abdu Saeed, 15-year-old Hafsa, and five-year-old Ola.

Five other family members were wounded, including a ten-year-old child. The injuries included shrapnel wounds to the head, ears, and limbs, as well as other wounds of varying severity.

The bodies of the martyrs were recovered from beneath the rubble of the destroyed house.

The family lost one woman and three young girls in a single Saudi airstrike, in another attack that struck civilians inside their homes.

suez.t: October 23, 1942. At twenty minutes to ten at night, in the desert of Egypt, more than eight hundred British guns open fire at once, and the darkness erupts in…
suez.tx:
October 23, 1942. At twenty minutes to ten at night, in the desert of Egypt, more than eight hundred British guns open fire at once, and the darkness erupts into a wall of flame and thunder that can be felt in the chest from miles away. The Second Battle of El Alamein has begun. It is the battle that will finally break Rommel in the desert, the hinge of the whole war in North Africa, and the victory that Churchill would say marked "the end of the beginning."

I have been following the desert war since the early days of this series, Rommel the Desert Fox running the British ragged back and forth across Libya and Egypt, the see-saw campaign that had swung all the way to El Alamein, the last defensible line before the Nile, the Suez Canal, and the oil of the Middle East. In the summer Rommel had been stopped there, barely, in the first battle. Now the British Eighth Army had a new commander, Bernard Montgomery, a careful, methodical, supremely confident general who had rebuilt the army's morale and refused to attack until he had overwhelming strength.

And by October he had it. Montgomery had built up a crushing superiority, in men, in tanks, in guns, in aircraft, in supplies, far more than Rommel could match, because the Axis supply line across the Mediterranean was being strangled while the British were pouring reinforcements, including masses of new American-built Sherman tanks, into Egypt. Rommel himself was away sick in Germany when the blow fell, his army dug in behind vast belts of mines and wire the Germans grimly called the "Devil's Gardens."

Montgomery's plan was not clever maneuver but deliberate, grinding attrition, a battle he called "crumbling." It opened on the night of the 23rd with one of the greatest artillery bombardments since the First World War, those eight hundred-plus guns firing in a stupendous barrage that announced the offensive and smashed at the Axis positions. Then the infantry went in, in the moonlight, to clear paths through the enormous minefields so the armor could pass, and the fighting settled into a brutal, close-quarters slog through the mines and the dug-in defenses.

It was not quick. For days the battle hung in the balance, the British grinding forward yard by yard through the Devil's Gardens, taking heavy losses, the attack at times seeming to stall. Rommel rushed back from Germany to take command, but he had no answer to Montgomery's material superiority and his relentless pressure, and critically he was running out of fuel, his tanks increasingly immobilized for lack of petrol. Montgomery kept up the attrition, wearing the Axis forces down, destroying tanks he could replace and Rommel could not, until at last, in early November, he concentrated his armor and punched through.

Rommel's front broke. Against Hitler's furious orders to stand and die, Rommel, to save what was left of his army, began a long retreat westward across the desert, a withdrawal that would not stop for hundreds of miles. The Axis army in the desert had been decisively beaten for the first time, and it would never recover the initiative. Combined with the Anglo-American landings in northwest Africa that came just days later, El Alamein doomed the entire Axis position in North Africa.

The victory meant an enormous amount, and not just militarily. It was the first great, clear-cut British land victory over the Germans in the whole war, coming after years of defeats and retreats, and it was desperately needed for Allied morale. Church bells were rung in Britain to celebrate. Churchill captured its meaning in one of his famous lines: "Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning." The tide in the west had turned, and it turned here, in the desert, beginning with those eight hundred guns firing into the dark on the night of the 23rd.

suez.t: 70 years ago today, on the 22nd of October 1956, France, Britain and Israel started negotiating a sinister deal at Sèvres. Israel would attack Egypt. France an…
suez.tx:
70 years ago today, on the 22nd of October 1956, France, Britain and Israel started negotiating a sinister deal at Sèvres. Israel would attack Egypt. France and Britain would order both sides to retreat. Nasser would refuse. France and Britain would then a have a casus belli to bomb Egypt. 

On 30 October 1956, Britain and France issued an ultimatum to Egypt and Israel. Stop fighting, withdraw your armies from the Suez Canal, or we will intervene to restore peace.

Sounds ever so benign, right? 

Or ever so cunning. 

They had secretly arranged the war themselves.

A few months earlier, Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser had nationalised the Suez Canal Company, which had been controlled by British and French interests.

The canal was on Egyptian territory, but Britain and France were used to deciding what happened there.

Nasser wanted the canal's revenues to help finance the Aswan High Dam, after the USA and Britain withdrew their offers to help finance its construction.

London was furious. 

Paris was 'pas amusé' either to say the least. French elites had special beef with Nasser over his support for the Algerian struggle against French colonial rule.

Israel had its own reasons to confront Egypt, including Egyptian restrictions on Israeli shipping and violent cross-border conflict.

Three governments with different grievances came together in one of history's most cynical ways. 

On 22 October 1956, senior representatives of Britain, France and Israel gathered secretly at Sèvres, outside Paris.

Among the Israeli participants were Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion, Moshe Dayan and Shimon Peres.

Over the following days they worked out a devious plan.

Israel would invade Egypt's Sinai Peninsula.

Britain and France would then demand that both sides withdraw from the Suez Canal.

Egypt would have to withdraw its forces from part of its own territory and allow foreign troops to occupy strategic positions along the canal.

The planners expected Nasser to refuse.

That refusal would give Britain and France their excuse to attack Egypt.

The agreement was signed on 24 October.

Five days later, Israel invaded.

On 30 October, Britain and France delivered their ultimatum.

The following day, British and French aircraft began bombing Egyptian targets.

Port Said got treated to bombardment, fighting and civilian casualties.

But then the plan ran into obstacles.

American president Dwight Eisenhower refused to support the operation. 

Washington applied enormous diplomatic and financial pressure. 

The Soviet Union threatened intervention.

Britain and France accepted a ceasefire on 6 November.

The invasion became a political humiliation. Nasser remained in power, and Egypt retained control of the canal.

It wasn't bad enough. Officials had to add shameless hypocrisy to the mix. 

On 20 December 1956, British Prime Minister Anthony Eden told the House of Commons that his government had possessed no foreknowledge that Israel would attack Egypt.

Yet British representatives had participated in the negotiations specifying precisely when Israel would attack.

The British diplomat who signed the secret agreement, Patrick Dean, had even returned to Paris the following day in an effort to destroy copies of the document.

Mortifying. 

Israel had to add sickening cruelty to the stinking cocktail. 

On 3 November 1956, during Israel's invasion of Egypt, Israeli troops occupied Khan Yunis in Gaza. There 275 Palestinians were reported killed, according to the UN. 

Palestinian witnesses described the killing of unarmed civilians, while Israel claimed its soldiers had encountered armed resistance.

Abdel Aziz al-Rantisi, 9 at the time, could hear the whole town wailing and wailing. Joe Sacco and Chris Hedges spoke to him decades ago and recently mentioned this haunting detail at a talk about their new book, Requiem for Gaza. 

That's how it goes. Elites hatch neat plans in warm rooms with delicious food, apathetic to who will be squished.

Building them in North Carolina creates real jobs, strengthens the industrial base, and reduces the leverage any foreign power has over our technology and security.
It’s not just about one state. It’s about making sure the devices we use every day and the systems that protect the country are no longer held hostage by geography or geopolitics. American manufacturing, American workers, American control of the technology that runs the 21st century. That’s the actual substance behind the announcement.

taiwan-strait.t: Gideon Rachman asks whether the world is “sleepwalking into World War III?” It’s a long read, and not a terribly enlightening one. Rachman tours Ukraine, the G…
taiwan-strait.tx:
Gideon Rachman asks whether the world is “sleepwalking into World War III?”

It’s a long read, and not a terribly enlightening one. Rachman tours Ukraine, the Gulf, the Taiwan Strait and the 65 conflicts currently raging around the world, and finds the culprits to be “revisionist powers”, “strongman leaders” and an “axis of adversaries”: Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

In a couple of thousand words, he finds no space at all for the crisis of neoliberal capitalism, albeit he does note the important fact that the G7, which accounted for two-thirds of world output in 1989, is now down to 43 percent.

Lenin would have recognised the connection between this decline and the attempt by declining powers to use military means to hold on to a world they can no longer dominate economically. He would have easily recognised “the striving for domination, not for freedom”.

More than a century after his death, Lenin remains a far better and more relevant guide to the questions of war and peace than the FT’s chief foreign affairs commentator.

Imperialism is hitting out in all directions:

• Genocide in Gaza, armed and financed by Washington, London and Berlin.

• US-Israeli criminal war on Iran and Lebanon.

• A proxy war in Ukraine to weaken and dismember Russia.

• Economic warfare against China: tariffs, chip bans, sanctions, blacklists.

• A “Donroe Doctrine” under which a president is kidnapped, Cuba is placed under a genocidal energy siege, and election results are determined in Washington DC.

• AUKUS, RIMPAC, Talisman Sabre, and a ring of US bases around China’s coast.

None of this features as a cause of insecurity in Rachman’s telling. He’s more worried about whether Xi Jinping “considers that America’s Taiwan Relations Act means something”, or whether Putin sees NATO’s Article Five as an “iconclad commitment”.

In other words, his proposed path to peace is for the US to make its threats more credible. Peace through NATO. Peace through imperialism.

The real guarantee of peace is a multipolar world where no power gets to dictate terms to the rest – exactly what Rachman’s “axis of adversaries” is working towards, and exactly what the West is fighting to prevent.
